title: Authentication in the App Router
summary: Authentication in the Next.js App Router is about **establishing a session** (cookie or JWT), then **checking it in the right place** — middleware for coarse gating, Server Components and a shared `auth()` helper for reading the user, and a re-check inside every Server Action and Route Handler because UI gating is never security.

subtopics.title: Sessions vs JWT
subtopics.explanation: Two ways to remember a logged-in user. A stateful SESSION stores a random opaque ID in a cookie and keeps the real data server-side (DB/Redis); it is easy to revoke but needs a lookup per request. A stateless JWT packs signed claims into the cookie itself — no lookup, but you cannot instantly revoke it and must keep it small. Most Next apps use a session cookie or a short-lived JWT plus a refresh strategy.
subtopics.example:
// session: cookie holds a random id -> server looks up the user
// jwt: cookie holds signed { sub, role, exp } -> server just verifies the signature

subtopics.title: httpOnly cookies
subtopics.explanation: The session token should live in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so client JavaScript can never read it (defeating XSS token theft) and the browser attaches it automatically to same-site requests. Storing tokens in localStorage exposes them to any injected script. In Next you set this with cookies().set() in a Server Action or Route Handler.
subtopics.example: cookies().set('session', token, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', path: '/' });

subtopics.title: Middleware vs layout vs Server Component
subtopics.explanation: Middleware runs at the edge before rendering and is great for CHEAP, COARSE gating (redirect unauthenticated users away from /dashboard/*) — but it should only check token presence/shape, not hit a database. Layouts and Server Components read the real session for rendering decisions (show the user's name, hide admin links). The actual authorization for a mutation belongs in the Server Action / Route Handler, not the layout.

subtopics.title: Reading the session in a Server Component
subtopics.explanation: Server Components run only on the server, so they can read the cookie and resolve the user directly with no client round-trip and no token exposure. Centralize this in one cached helper (e.g. an `auth()` function) so every Server Component, Action, and Handler resolves the user the same way and you only verify once per request.
subtopics.example:
const session = await auth(); if (!session) redirect('/login'); return

Hello {session.user.name}

;

subtopics.title: Auth.js / NextAuth overview
subtopics.explanation: Auth.js (formerly NextAuth) is the de-facto library: you configure providers (OAuth, email, credentials), it manages the session cookie/JWT and CSRF, and exposes an `auth()` helper plus `signIn`/`signOut`. It wires a catch-all Route Handler at app/api/auth/[...nextauth] and a middleware export. You still write your own authorization (which user can do what) on top of the identity it provides.
subtopics.example: export const { auth, handlers, signIn, signOut } = NextAuth({ providers: [GitHub] });

subtopics.title: Server Actions + auth
subtopics.explanation: A Server Action is a callable server endpoint — anyone who can reach the page can invoke it. So the FIRST lines of every action must re-establish identity and check permission; never trust a hidden field, the referring page, or the fact that the button was only shown to admins. Auth in the action is the real security boundary.
subtopics.example: async function deletePost(id) { 'use server'; const s = await auth(); if (s?.user.role !== 'admin') throw new Error('Forbidden'); /* ... */ }

subtopics.title: Role-based access control (RBAC)
subtopics.explanation: Once identity is known, authorization decides WHAT they may do. RBAC attaches roles (user/editor/admin) or permissions to the session and checks them centrally — ideally one `can(user, action, resource)` helper reused by UI (to hide controls) and by every Action/Handler (to enforce). UI hiding is convenience; the server check is the gate.

subtopics.title: CSRF and same-site protection
subtopics.explanation: Because cookies are sent automatically, a malicious site could trigger an authenticated request (CSRF). SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies block most cross-site POSTs; Auth.js also issues CSRF tokens for its forms. Server Actions are POST-only with an action-id check, which mitigates basic CSRF, but for custom cookie-auth mutations you still verify origin/SameSite and avoid GET mutations.
subtopics.example: // SameSite=lax blocks cross-site POST cookies; verify Origin header on sensitive routes

foundations.overview: Authentication answers 'who is this request from?' and authorization answers 'are they allowed to do this?'. In the App Router you establish a session (a signed cookie holding a session id or a JWT), then resolve and check it across several layers — middleware for cheap gating, Server Components/layouts for rendering the right UI, and Server Actions/Route Handlers for the real enforcement of every mutation and data read.
foundations.formalDefinition: Authentication is the process of verifying a principal's identity and binding it to a request via a credential (a session cookie referencing server state, or a self-contained signed JWT). Authorization is the subsequent decision of whether that authenticated principal may perform a requested action on a resource.
foundations.whyItMatters: Getting auth wrong is the most common source of serious security bugs — leaked tokens, broken access control, and CSRF. In Next specifically, the Server/Client split and Server Actions create new places to forget the check, so understanding WHERE each layer enforces what is essential.
foundations.mentalModel: Think in three rings: (1) middleware = the bouncer at the door doing a quick ID glance (presence/shape only), (2) Server Components = the host who reads your badge to personalize the room, (3) Server Actions/Route Handlers = the vault door that actually verifies you may take an action. Only the vault door is security.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser stores the session in an httpOnly cookie it cannot read from JS and attaches it automatically to same-site requests. The client never sees the raw token; it only sees rendered HTML and the results of server calls, which is why secrets and authorization stay on the server.
foundations.realWorldUsage: A SaaS app uses Auth.js with an OAuth provider, stores a session cookie, gates /app/* in middleware, reads the user in the dashboard layout to show the right nav, and re-checks role in every Server Action that mutates data.
foundations.businessImpact: Solid auth protects customer data and meets compliance (SOC 2, GDPR), while a single broken-access-control bug can mean a breach, fines, and lost trust. Smooth OAuth/passwordless flows also directly improve signup conversion.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Centralizing identity in one `auth()` helper and authorization in one `can()` helper keeps checks consistent and auditable; scattering ad-hoc cookie reads and role checks guarantees a forgotten gate eventually ships.
foundations.performanceImpact: Stateful sessions add a per-request store lookup (cache it, e.g. React cache() per request); stateless JWTs avoid the lookup but cannot be revoked instantly. Edge middleware keeps gating cheap, but doing DB calls there hurts every request — keep it to token verification.
commonUseCases: OAuth/social login via Auth.js with a session cookie
Gating an entire /dashboard segment in middleware
Reading the current user in a layout to render the right navigation
Re-checking role inside Server Actions before mutating data

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the page is only shown to admins, the Server Action behind it is safe.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A Server Action is a public POST endpoint. Anyone can invoke it directly, so it must re-verify identity and permission itself — hiding the button is not security.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Middleware is where you enforce authorization.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Middleware is for cheap, coarse redirects based on token presence/shape. Real authorization (and DB checks) belongs in Server Components for reads and Actions/Route Handlers for writes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Storing the JWT in localStorage is fine.
commonMisconceptions.reality: localStorage is readable by any injected script, so an XSS leaks the token. Use an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie the browser sends automatically.

config.intro: Trace an authenticated request through middleware, the layout, a Server Component, and a Server Action.

steps.name: Middleware (edge)
steps.detail: Runs first. Reads the session cookie and checks it EXISTS and is well-formed. No DB call. Missing/invalid -> redirect to /login. This is coarse gating only.

steps.name: Layout (Server Component)
steps.detail: auth() resolves the real user from the cookie/store once per request. Used to render the correct nav, hide admin links, and personalize — a rendering decision, not the security gate.

steps.name: Page Server Component
steps.detail: Reuses the cached session to fetch only data this user may see. Because it runs server-side, the token never reaches the browser and data access stays on the server.

steps.name: Server Action (mutation)
steps.detail: User clicks 'Delete'. The action re-runs auth() and can(user, 'delete', resource). THIS is the real enforcement — it does not trust that the UI was hidden.

steps.name: Route Handler (API)
steps.detail: External/3rd-party callers hit a Route Handler instead; it verifies the session or an API token the same way before responding, so every entry point is gated.

debuggingLab.title: The Server Action trusts the UI
debuggingLab.symptom: Non-admin users can delete posts by replaying the network request, even though the Delete button is hidden for them.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A Server Action is a public POST endpoint. Hiding the Delete button in the client only changes what is rendered — anyone can invoke the action directly (e.g. replaying the request). With no auth()/role check inside the action, any authenticated user (or even any caller who guesses the action) can delete. UI gating is never the security boundary.
commonMistakes: Assuming a hidden button means the action behind it is protected.
Checking the role in middleware or the layout but not inside the action itself.
Trusting a hidden form field or the referring page to convey authorization.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Re-resolve the session inside the action and reject anyone who is not an admin before touching the database.

theory.question: Sessions vs JWT for auth in a Next.js app — what are the trade-offs and which would you pick?
theory.directAnswer: A stateful session stores a random id in an httpOnly cookie and keeps the user data server-side, so it is trivial to revoke but needs a per-request lookup (cache it). A stateless JWT puts signed claims in the cookie, avoiding the lookup but making instant revocation hard and risking staleness. For most apps I default to a session (or a short-lived JWT plus refresh) in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, because revocability and not exposing claims usually matter more than skipping one cached lookup.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two credential strategies: server-stored session referenced by an opaque cookie id, vs a self-contained signed token carrying the claims.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To remember an authenticated user across stateless HTTP requests, trading revocability against statelessness/scale.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Session: cookie id -> store lookup -> user. JWT: verify signature + exp on the token itself, no store. Either way the token lives in an httpOnly cookie the browser sends automatically.

theory.whyImportant: It is a foundational design choice that affects revocation, scale, and security, and is a near-universal senior interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: Banking app uses server sessions for instant revocation on logout/compromise; a high-scale read-heavy API may use short-lived JWTs with refresh tokens to avoid per-request lookups.

nestedTopics.title: Revocation
nestedTopics.explanation: Sessions revoke by deleting the store row; JWTs need a denylist or short expiry + refresh to approximate it.

nestedTopics.title: Where to store it
nestedTopics.explanation: Always an httpOnly Secure cookie, never localStorage, so XSS cannot read the token.

nestedTopics.title: Per-request cost
nestedTopics.explanation: Sessions add a store lookup; wrap auth() in React cache() so it resolves once per request.

followUps.question: How do you make a session lookup cheap in the App Router?
followUps.answer: Centralize it in an auth() helper wrapped in React's cache() so the cookie is verified and the user resolved once per request and reused across layout, page, and actions.

followUps.question: How do you revoke a JWT before it expires?
followUps.answer: Keep them short-lived and use a server-side denylist (e.g. by jti) or rotate a refresh token; pure stateless JWTs cannot be instantly revoked.

theory.question: Where should you check authentication and authorization in the App Router — middleware, layout, Server Component, or Server Action?
theory.directAnswer: Use middleware for cheap, coarse gating (redirect unauthenticated users away from a segment based only on token presence/shape — no DB). Use layouts/Server Components to read the real session for RENDERING decisions. But the actual security enforcement for every read and write belongs in the Server Component that fetches data and in every Server Action / Route Handler that mutates — because those are the genuine entry points and Server Actions are public POST endpoints. Never rely on middleware or hidden UI as the authorization gate.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A layered model: middleware (door), Server Components (personalization), Actions/Handlers (vault).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Each layer runs at a different time/cost; placing the cheap check early and the real check at the entry point keeps both performance and security correct.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Middleware verifies token shape at the edge; auth() in RSC/layout resolves the user for rendering; the action/handler re-verifies and authorizes before any data operation.

theory.whyImportant: Misplacing the gate (e.g. enforcing only in middleware or trusting hidden UI) is the classic broken-access-control bug in Next apps.
theory.realWorldExample: A /admin segment: middleware redirects non-logged-in users; the admin layout reads the session to render the panel; each admin Server Action re-checks role === 'admin' before mutating.

nestedTopics.title: Why not enforce in middleware
nestedTopics.explanation: It runs at the edge without your DB, can be bypassed for non-matched paths, and is meant for routing, not fine-grained authorization.

nestedTopics.title: Defense in depth
nestedTopics.explanation: Check at each layer, but treat the Action/Handler check as the single source of truth for security.

followUps.question: Can middleware do the full authorization check?
followUps.answer: No — it should avoid DB calls and runs only for matched routes; use it for coarse redirects and enforce real authz at the data/mutation layer.

scenario.question: A security review finds that any logged-in user can call admin-only Server Actions even though the admin UI is hidden from them. How do you fix it and prevent recurrence?
scenario.directAnswer: The root cause is treating the hidden UI as the gate. I'd add an authorization check at the start of every Server Action and Route Handler — resolve the session with auth() and call a central can(user, action, resource) before any mutation. To prevent recurrence I'd centralize identity and authorization in shared helpers, add a 'requireRole' wrapper used by all actions, write tests that invoke actions directly as a non-admin and assert they throw, and treat UI hiding as UX only.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A broken-access-control bug: missing server-side authorization on a public action endpoint.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Teams often gate in the UI/middleware and forget the action is independently callable.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Adding auth()+can() at the action boundary makes the server the single enforcement point; a shared wrapper makes it hard to forget.

scenario.whyImportant: Broken access control is consistently a top web vulnerability and a frequent senior-interview scenario.

nestedTopics.title: requireRole wrapper
nestedTopics.explanation: A higher-order helper that wraps an action and throws unless the session satisfies the role/permission.

nestedTopics.title: Tests as a safety net
nestedTopics.explanation: Invoke actions directly as different roles and assert the unauthorized ones are rejected.

followUps.question: How would you audit the codebase for other unprotected actions?
followUps.answer: Lint/grep for 'use server' files lacking an auth()/requireRole call, and require the wrapper in code review and CI.

coding.question: Write a reusable Server Action wrapper that enforces a required role before running the action.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want one place to resolve the session and check the role so individual actions cannot forget it. A higher-order function takes a required role and the action body, resolves auth(), throws on failure, and otherwise calls the body with the session. This makes the security check declarative and consistent.
coding.lineByLine: requireRole is a higher-order function: it takes the required role and the real action body. The returned function resolves the session via auth(); if there is no user it throws Unauthenticated, and if the role does not match (admins always pass) it throws Forbidden. Only then does it call the action with the verified session. deletePost is declared by wrapping the body, so the check can never be forgotten.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) plus the cost of auth() (a cached session lookup per request).

alternativeApproaches.title: Permission-based instead of role-based
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Check a fine-grained permission via can(user, action, resource) rather than a coarse role, which scales better as rules grow.

followUps.question: How would you surface 'Forbidden' to the user nicely?
followUps.answer: Catch the thrown error in the calling component / form action state and render a friendly message, while still failing closed on the server.

systemDesign.question: Design the authentication and authorization system for a multi-tenant Next.js (App Router) SaaS with social login, an admin area, and a public API.
systemDesign.directAnswer: I'd use Auth.js for identity (OAuth + email providers) issuing an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite session cookie, with the session enriched to carry userId, tenantId, and role. A central auth() helper (React-cached per request) resolves the session everywhere. Middleware does coarse gating of /app/* and /admin/* by token presence. Reads are authorized inside Server Components scoped by tenantId; writes go through Server Actions wrapped in requireRole/can() that enforce both tenant isolation and RBAC. The public API uses Route Handlers authenticated by API keys/bearer tokens with the same authorization helpers. Sessions are revocable (server store), secrets stay server-side, and every entry point shares one authorization layer.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An end-to-end auth design covering identity, session, multi-tenant isolation, RBAC, and a public API surface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A SaaS needs strong tenant isolation, flexible login, and a single consistent authorization model across UI and API.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Auth.js authenticates and sets the session cookie; auth() resolves {userId, tenantId, role}; middleware coarse-gates; Server Components filter all queries by tenantId; Server Actions/Route Handlers enforce can()/requireRole and re-assert tenant scope before any mutation.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Multi-tenant SaaS auth combines the highest-risk concerns (tenant data isolation + access control) and is a classic senior system-design prompt.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: Linear/Vercel-style dashboards: OAuth login, org/tenant in the session, role-scoped admin tools, and a token-authenticated public API sharing the same permission checks.

nestedTopics.title: Tenant isolation
nestedTopics.explanation: Every query must filter by the session's tenantId; never accept tenantId from the client. A shared data-access layer enforces this so no query can leak across tenants.

nestedTopics.title: Session model
nestedTopics.explanation: Server-side sessions (DB/Redis) keyed by an opaque cookie id give instant revocation on logout, role change, or compromise; cache resolution per request for performance.

nestedTopics.title: Public API auth
nestedTopics.explanation: Route Handlers accept scoped API keys/bearer tokens mapped to a tenant+permissions, reusing can() so UI and API share one authorization source of truth.

nestedTopics.title: Security hardening
nestedTopics.explanation: httpOnly/Secure/SameSite cookies, CSRF protection on forms, origin checks on sensitive routes, secrets only in server code, rate limiting on auth endpoints.

followUps.question: How do you handle a user belonging to multiple tenants?
followUps.answer: Store the active tenantId in the session and let the user switch tenants (re-issuing/updating the session), while every query and action validates membership in that tenant before proceeding.

followUps.question: Where do you enforce tenant isolation so it can't be forgotten?
followUps.answer: In a single data-access layer that always injects the session's tenantId into queries, so individual pages/actions cannot accidentally query across tenants.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Centralize identity in one auth() helper (React-cached per request) and authorization in one can()/requireRole layer reused by Server Components (reads), Server Actions (writes), and Route Handlers (API). Middleware does only cheap coarse gating. A shared data-access layer injects tenant scope so isolation can't be forgotten. Auth.js manages providers, the session cookie, and CSRF.
productionDeepDive.performance: Cache session resolution per request so the layout, page, and actions don't each hit the session store. Keep middleware free of DB calls. Prefer short-lived tokens with refresh for very high-scale read paths, but accept the per-request lookup for revocable sessions in most apps.
productionDeepDive.security: Store tokens in httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies — never localStorage. Treat every Server Action/Route Handler as a public endpoint requiring its own authz check. Keep secrets and access logic server-side, validate input, protect against CSRF (SameSite + tokens, origin checks), and fail closed.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Server-side sessions need a fast store (Redis) and revocation list as users grow; multi-tenant apps must guarantee tenant-scoped queries. Rate-limit auth and sensitive mutation endpoints to resist brute force and abuse.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Force every mutation through a requireRole/can wrapper so the check can't be omitted; lint for 'use server' files missing an auth call; document the role/permission model in one place so reviewers can reason about it.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log auth events (login, logout, role change, forbidden) with userId/tenantId; alert on spikes in 'Forbidden' or failed logins; monitor session store latency and token verification errors.

caseStudies.problem: Admin-only Server Actions were callable by any logged-in user because gating lived only in the UI/middleware.
caseStudies.solution: Introduced a requireRole wrapper and a tenant-scoped data-access layer enforced in every action and handler, with tests invoking actions as each role.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more boilerplate per action vs guaranteed, auditable enforcement.
caseStudies.lessons: UI hiding and middleware are not security; the real gate must sit at every server entry point and be impossible to forget.

projectBuilder.summary: Add authentication and RBAC to the SaaS app: social login, a gated dashboard, role-scoped admin actions, and a token-authenticated public API.
requirements: Users log in via Auth.js (OAuth) and get an httpOnly session cookie
Middleware redirects anonymous users away from /app/*
Every Server Action enforces role/permission before mutating
A public Route Handler authenticates via API token using the same authz helpers
projectBuilder.architecture: Auth.js issues a session cookie; a cached auth() helper resolves {userId, tenantId, role} everywhere; middleware coarse-gates; Server Components read tenant-scoped data; Server Actions and Route Handlers enforce can()/requireRole.

steps.title: Configure Auth.js
steps.instructions: Set up providers and export auth/handlers/signIn/signOut; wire the catch-all Route Handler.
steps.checkpoint: Login sets an httpOnly session cookie and auth() returns the user.

steps.title: Gate routes
steps.instructions: Add middleware that redirects unauthenticated users from /app/* and /admin/* based on token presence only.

steps.title: Enforce authorization
steps.instructions: Read the session in the dashboard layout for rendering, and wrap every mutating action in requireRole/can.
steps.checkpoint: A non-admin invoking an admin action (even directly) is rejected with Forbidden.

steps.title: Secure the public API
steps.instructions: Add a Route Handler authenticated by API token that reuses the same authorization helpers and tenant scope.
steps.checkpoint: API requests without a valid token are rejected; valid ones are tenant-scoped.

Add an admin audit log of forbidden attempts
Add tenant switching for multi-tenant users
interviewQuestions: Why is the role check inside the Server Action rather than in middleware?
How do you guarantee every query is scoped to the user's tenant?

keyTakeaways: Authentication establishes identity (a session or JWT in an httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie); authorization decides what that identity may do.
Check auth in layers: middleware for cheap coarse gating, Server Components for rendering, and Server Actions/Route Handlers for the real enforcement — UI hiding and middleware are NOT security.
A Server Action is a public POST endpoint: re-resolve the session and check role/permission at the start of every one.
Centralize identity in a cached auth() helper and authorization in a requireRole/can() layer reused everywhere, including a tenant-scoped data-access layer for multi-tenant apps.
Never store tokens in localStorage; use httpOnly cookies, keep secrets server-side, and protect against CSRF with SameSite cookies, tokens, and origin checks.
